title: Heart Failure & Acute Pulmonary Edema: Congestion, Perfusion and Decompensation Rescue
html:
Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which structural or functional cardiac impairment prevents the heart from filling or ejecting effectively enough to meet the body's needs without elevated pressures. The RN translates a changing pattern of congestion and perfusion into timely action. Ejection fraction helps classify heart failure, but it does not replace bedside assessment: a client can be critically ill with either reduced or preserved ejection fraction.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate left- and right-sided findings, congestion and hypoperfusion, and chronic compensation from acute decompensation.
  • Explain HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF, and improved ejection fraction without treating EF as the whole diagnosis.
  • Recognize acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock and prioritize immediate nursing actions.
  • Monitor diuretics, vasodilators, vasoactive therapy, and guideline-directed chronic medications safely.
  • Use weights, intake and output, symptoms, renal function, and electrolytes to evaluate response.
  • Teach an individualized home-monitoring and escalation plan using teach-back.

Heart failure is a pressure, volume, and perfusion problem

Reduced forward flow activates the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. These responses initially support blood pressure and perfusion but also increase heart rate, vasoconstriction, sodium and water retention, preload, afterload, and myocardial workload. Ventricular remodeling can further impair function. A client may therefore cycle between compensation and decompensation.

Preload reflects ventricular filling and stretch; too little can reduce output, while excessive filling pressure promotes congestion. Afterload is the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Contractility is the myocardium's pumping force. Nursing assessment links these concepts to symptoms, vital signs, lung and neck-vein findings, edema, urine output, mentation, and medication response rather than relying on one hemodynamic term.

Ejection fraction classifies—not fully describes—heart failure

HFrEF has reduced left-ventricular ejection fraction, generally 40% or less. HFmrEF has mildly reduced EF, generally 41% to 49%, with evidence of elevated filling pressure. HFpEF generally has EF of 50% or more with evidence of elevated filling pressure; impaired relaxation and stiffness can cause severe congestion even though the percentage ejected appears preserved. HF with improved EF describes a prior reduced EF that later rises above 40%; improvement does not mean the disease or treatment need has disappeared.

Also distinguish guideline stages from symptom classes. Stages describe disease progression from risk through advanced heart failure; functional class describes activity limitation at the time assessed. Do not interchange them or infer severity from EF alone.

Separate congestion from low perfusion

Left-sided congestion can produce exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, crackles, hypoxemia, an S3, or pulmonary edema. Right-sided congestion can produce jugular venous distention, dependent edema, ascites, abdominal fullness, hepatomegaly, nausea, and weight gain. Both often coexist because the ventricles and circulation are connected.

Low-output findings include cool or mottled skin, weak pulses, narrow pulse pressure, fatigue, dizziness, altered mentation, oliguria, rising lactate, and worsening kidney or liver function. Blood pressure can be normal early, and edema can coexist with poor effective perfusion. Classify the pattern dynamically: congested or not, adequately perfused or not, stable or deteriorating.

Edema does not guarantee adequate circulation
A client can have excess total-body fluid and still have low organ perfusion. Do not automatically give or withhold fluid from one sign; integrate lungs, neck veins, pressure, perfusion, urine, weight, labs, and response.

Find the reason for decompensation

Common triggers include acute coronary syndrome, uncontrolled hypertension, dysrhythmia, infection, kidney injury, anemia, pulmonary embolism, thyroid disease, medication interruption, medications that worsen fluid retention or cardiac function, excess sodium or fluid intake, and progression of valve or myocardial disease. Ask about symptom onset, functional change, medication access and adherence without blame, recent illness, diet, weight trend, substance exposure, and care barriers.

Compare current status with the client's baseline: usual weight, activity, sleep position, edema, blood pressure, heart rate, rhythm, renal function, oxygen use, and diuretic response. A subtle decline in walking distance or need for another pillow may precede obvious respiratory distress.

Acute pulmonary edema is an oxygenation emergency

Sudden severe dyspnea, tachypnea, anxiety, diaphoresis, diffuse crackles, hypoxemia, inability to lie flat, and pink frothy sputum suggest alveolar flooding. Sit the client upright when tolerated, call for emergency support, assess ABCs and perfusion, apply oxygen for hypoxemia, establish continuous cardiac and oxygen monitoring, obtain IV access, and prepare positive-pressure ventilation when indicated. Do not force the client flat for a routine examination.

Anticipate rapid evaluation for ACS, hypertensive emergency, dysrhythmia, acute valve failure, infection, and other causes. Prescribed IV loop diuretic and vasodilator therapy may reduce congestion and filling pressure when blood pressure supports their use. Closely reassess breathing, oxygenation, pressure, rhythm, urine output, symptoms, electrolytes, and kidney function. Morphine is not routine treatment for acute pulmonary edema.

Cardiogenic shock is more than a low blood pressure

Cardiogenic shock is inadequate tissue perfusion from cardiac pump failure. Findings can include hypotension, altered mentation, cool clammy skin, weak pulses, oliguria, rising lactate, metabolic acidosis, pulmonary congestion, and worsening organ function. Some clients maintain pressure temporarily through intense vasoconstriction, so trend the whole perfusion pattern.

Activate emergency and critical-care support, optimize oxygenation and ventilation, obtain hemodynamic and laboratory data, identify reversible causes, and prepare prescribed vasoactive or mechanical circulatory support. Urgent revascularization is central when acute MI is the cause. Fluids are individualized; repeated empiric boluses can worsen pulmonary edema, while selected clients may need cautious preload support under close reassessment.

Diagnostic data answer different questions

ECG assesses rhythm, conduction, and possible ischemia. Chest imaging can show pulmonary congestion or alternate disease. Echocardiography evaluates chamber structure, valve function, wall motion, filling clues, and EF. Natriuretic peptides support diagnosis and prognosis but are influenced by age, kidney function, obesity, rhythm, and treatment. A low value may make heart failure less likely in the right setting, while an elevated value is not diagnostic by itself.

Trend CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, glucose, kidney and liver function, troponin when indicated, thyroid studies when relevant, and arterial or venous blood gases in severe illness. Evaluate the test in context and avoid delaying stabilization while waiting for confirmation.

Diuresis requires a response-and-harm loop

Before and during loop-diuretic therapy, assess pressure, congestion, urine output, kidney function, sodium, potassium, magnesium, hearing risk with high-dose or rapid IV exposure, and the timing of prior doses. Use accurate intake and output and a consistent daily weight. Evaluate urine response, dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, neck veins, lungs, oxygen need, and function.

A rising creatinine during decongestion requires clinical interpretation; it does not automatically mean all diuresis must stop if congestion remains dangerous. Conversely, escalating diuretics despite hypotension, severe electrolyte loss, minimal response, or worsening perfusion may cause harm. Communicate the entire trend and follow the individualized plan.

Chronic HFrEF treatment changes outcomes

Guideline-directed therapy for symptomatic chronic HFrEF commonly builds on four medication classes: an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, ACE inhibitor, or ARB as appropriate; an evidence-based beta blocker; a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Diuretics relieve congestion but serve a different purpose from medications that reduce long-term morbidity and mortality. Other therapies may be indicated for selected clients.

Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, rhythm, kidney function, potassium, volume status, glucose-related risks, and adverse effects appropriate to each drug. Beta blockers are usually started or adjusted when the client is clinically stable rather than during uncontrolled shock. Mineralocorticoid antagonists and renin-angiotensin system drugs can increase potassium. SGLT2 inhibitors can cause volume depletion and genital infection and may rarely contribute to ketoacidosis even without marked hyperglycemia; follow sick-day and peri-procedure instructions.

Do not stop chronic therapy simply because EF improves or symptoms resolve. Confirm the treatment plan with the qualified team, because withdrawal can allow relapse. Medication titration is individualized and often occurs over multiple visits.

HFpEF still requires active management

HFpEF is not mild heart failure. Treatment targets congestion and contributing conditions such as hypertension, atrial fibrillation, ischemia, obesity, diabetes, kidney disease, sleep-disordered breathing, and valve disease. SGLT2 inhibitors can reduce heart-failure hospitalization across a broad EF range in appropriate clients. Avoid assuming that therapies proven for HFrEF have identical benefit in HFpEF.

Prevent medication-related deterioration

Reconcile prescriptions, over-the-counter products, supplements, and recent changes. NSAIDs can promote sodium retention and kidney injury. Some nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, thiazolidinediones, and other medications may worsen selected forms of heart failure. Verify rather than independently discontinuing therapy, and communicate hypotension, bradycardia, kidney change, hyperkalemia, dehydration, or new congestion promptly.

Avoid routine rapid IV fluid for every episode of oliguria or hypotension. Likewise, do not apply a universal sodium or fluid restriction; targets depend on symptoms, comorbidities, medications, and the care plan.

Devices and advanced therapy need safety teaching

Selected clients may benefit from an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, cardiac resynchronization, valve intervention, ventricular assist device, transplant evaluation, or palliative support. After an implantable-device procedure, monitor the site, rhythm, symptoms, and procedure-specific activity instructions. A shock accompanied by persistent symptoms, repeated shocks, syncope, or instability requires emergency evaluation.

For advanced heart failure, goals-of-care discussions and palliative care can occur alongside disease-directed treatment. Clarify the client's values, surrogate decision maker, device preferences, symptom priorities, and emergency plan without equating palliative care with abandonment.

Daily trends make discharge safer

Teach the client to weigh under consistent conditions—commonly in the morning after voiding and before eating, using the same scale and similar clothing—and record the result. The client should follow the care team's individualized thresholds for calling; commonly used alerts include a rapid gain of about 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week, but the written personal plan takes priority.

Track worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, nighttime breathlessness, cough, swelling, abdominal fullness, fatigue, dizziness, confusion, palpitations, appetite, blood pressure or pulse when directed, and medication response. Teach which symptoms call for the heart-failure team and which require emergency services, including severe breathlessness at rest, fainting, new chest pressure, cyanosis, or marked confusion.

Use teach-back for medications, diet and fluid plan, daily monitoring, follow-up, and emergency actions. Address affordability, pharmacy access, transportation, food access, language, cognition, dexterity, and caregiver support before discharge. Refer to cardiac rehabilitation when appropriate and reinforce vaccination, tobacco cessation, activity progression, and comorbidity care.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Gather dyspnea pattern, sleep position, weight, edema, neck veins, lung sounds, oxygenation, pressure, rhythm, perfusion, urine, mentation, medications, diet, renal function, electrolytes, ECG, and imaging.
  2. Analyze cues: Determine whether the client is congested, hypoperfused, both, or neither; distinguish chronic baseline from acute change and identify likely triggers.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Acute pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, ACS, unstable dysrhythmia, severe electrolyte disturbance, and acute valve failure outrank routine teaching.
  4. Generate solutions: Support oxygenation and perfusion, position safely, activate emergency resources, treat the trigger, decongest when appropriate, and prevent medication harm.
  5. Take action: Implement protocol-directed monitoring and therapy, measure response accurately, protect against falls and hypotension, and escalate deterioration.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess breathing, oxygen need, perfusion, mentation, rhythm, pressure, weight, urine, congestion, kidney function, electrolytes, function, and self-management understanding.

Clinical example

A client with HFrEF arrives unable to lie flat, speaking in short phrases, with diffuse crackles, oxygen saturation 84%, cool skin, and a rapid weight gain. The RN sits the client upright, activates emergency support, applies oxygen and continuous monitoring, obtains IV access, and prepares positive-pressure ventilation and ordered IV therapy. Because the blood pressure is falling and urine output is low, the RN communicates both congestion and hypoperfusion, avoids an automatic fluid bolus, and reassesses oxygenation, work of breathing, pressure, rhythm, mentation, urine, electrolytes, and kidney function after each intervention.

Heart-failure diagnosis, ejection-fraction classification, oxygen targets, fluid and sodium plans, medication selection and titration, diuresis, vasoactive therapy, device care, and emergency treatment require current clinical data, authorized orders, local protocols, specialist input, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official ACC, AHA, HFSA, or NCSBN product.
